meta.status: Desk-sourced and draft profiles from published material and, for some, custodian-supplied material. None has been reviewed by any custodian or community. Not an official record.
meta.coordinate_note: Two sites have a location, each a bay-level point, not a boundary: one from published sources, and one from custodian-supplied material, generalised with the Field Kit's rule. Others are deliberately left unmapped until someone records a location with permission.

sites.name: Kira Forest Biodiversity Conservation Area (KFBCA)
sites.place_text: Kira tribal land, Takataka Bay; Kira Conservation Centre at Masupa village

location.note: Point is Takataka Bay, where the sources place Kira tribal land. It is NOT the protected-area boundary.

sites.summary_en: About 677 hectares of forest on Kira tribal land near Takataka Bay, declared a Protected Area under the national Protected Areas Act 2010. Sources describe it as the first in Malaita Province. Logging and mining are prohibited, and a community committee with rangers manages it.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Reported as 677 hectares (S01, S02, S03, S16), 667 hectares (S15) and 661 hectares (S18).
facts.note: 677 hectares is the figure given at the declaration. The sources do not agree, and none of the figures has been checked with the Kira committee.

facts.label: Legal status
facts.value: Declared a Protected Area under the Protected Areas Act 2010; registered as Resource Management Area Category 4 (Protected Areas Regulation 2012).
facts.note: Sources cite the Act as both 'Protected Areas Act 2010' and 'Protected Areas Management Act 2010'. Check the certificate.

facts.label: Declared
facts.value: October 2023. Ceremony at the Kira Conservation Centre.
facts.note: Sources conflict on the exact day. S01, S02 and S16 describe a ceremony on Friday 27 to Saturday 28 'November', but S16 was published on 2 November 2023, so this most likely means 27-28 October 2023. S15 gives 29 October 2023 for the declaration and also mentions a celebration on 27 November 2023. Confirm from the certificate.

facts.label: Claimed 'first'
facts.value: The first conservation group in Malaita Province to be declared a Protected Area. Nationally it appears to be the sixth legal Protected Area: five existed by July 2022, with Vuri the most recent, and the Kira announcement says six have been declared to date.
facts.note: An earlier version of this profile repeated S01's description of Kira as the first forest Protected Area by law in Solomon Islands. S12 and S28 contradict that, so it has been dropped. Check against the national Protected Area register.

facts.label: Management
facts.value: Kira Protected Area Management Committee and rangers, working to a management plan. Logging and mining are prohibited.
facts.note: The management plan has not been seen.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: Grew from the Taka' Taka Eco-Village Conservation Foundation, conceived in 2014 and legally registered on 11 March 2015 as an incorporated non-profit. The foundation works in wards 19 and 20 of East Are'are, around Takataka Bay.

facts.label: Partners named
facts.value: Winrock International (supplied GPS mapping equipment), Mai-Maasina Green Belt, Wai-Hau Conservation Foundation, Ahetaha Water Conservation Association.
facts.note: The last partner is called a 'Foundation' in S02 and an 'Association' in S04.

facts.label: Stated priorities
facts.value: Economic development, kastom education and environmental stewardship.

facts.label: Species and habitats
facts.value: Forest. A baseline assessment reported about 126 plant species and 70 wildlife species (11 amphibians, 11 reptiles, 32 birds, 9 mammals and 7 aquatic species), including 28 endemic birds. Solomon's sea eagle is listed as vulnerable.
facts.note: Figures as reported by the Equator Initiative. Parts of that page describe an unrelated project and were ignored. The full survey has not been seen.

facts.label: Community
facts.value: More than 300 households in Masupa, Aiarai and Purimou are reported to benefit. Kira land is described as among the last unlogged areas in Malaita.
facts.note: From a partner organisation's article. The 'last unlogged' description has not been checked.

facts.label: Carbon project
facts.value: A forest carbon project with Nakau Nature Connect is in development.
facts.note: From the project developer's own page. The Kira committee has not confirmed what may be shown about this project.

facts.label: Threats and pressures
facts.value: Not yet recorded in this profile.

visitor.note: A conservation centre exists at Masupa, but no visitor policy was found. Do not assume the area is open to visitors. Ask the Kira committee first.

contact.note: A site coordinator is named in S02. Not republished here until that person agrees to be listed.

consent.note: Prepared from published sources only. The Kira committee has not seen or approved this profile.

open_questions: On which days in October 2023 was the area declared, and where is the signed certificate?
Can the committee share its GPS boundary (made with the Winrock equipment) and agree on how it is shown publicly?
Is the management plan public, and does it say anything about visitors?
Have any biodiversity surveys been done, and may their findings be shown?
How are the rangers supported, and what do they need?
What are the rules and fees for a research or tourism visit, and who gives permission?
Which of the reported areas (677, 667 or 661 hectares) is correct, and how was it measured?
What may be shown publicly about the carbon project with Nakau? The Kira committee should confirm this before anything more is added.

sites.name: Ahetaha Water Conservation Association (AWCA)

location.note: No sourced coordinates for Ahetaha village. Needs a field location recorded with permission.

sites.summary_en: A community association at Ahetaha in East Are'are working to protect mangroves, reefs, seagrass, rainforest and freshwater. Chiefs set rules for designated areas in 2016. The group also mentors other conservation groups in East Are'are.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Not stated.

facts.label: Legal status
facts.value: No formal protected-area registration appears in the sources read. S04 notes that the few formal protected areas in Solomon Islands are mostly on tribal customary land with little management capacity.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: A chief formed the association after first persuading relatives to protect the mangroves and reefs along the seafront at Ahetaha.

facts.label: Rules
facts.value: In 2016 community chiefs set rules to protect designated areas.

facts.label: Focus
facts.value: Mangrove planting at the river mouth and seafront; dugong and green turtle recovery; seagrass management; rainforest and freshwater species.

facts.label: Customary practice
facts.value: Communities temporarily close reefs and fishing grounds, for example before feasts.
facts.note: Described by an outside organisation. The community should confirm how it wants this practice described.

facts.label: Threats and pressures
facts.value: Boat strikes, hunting for feasts and nets harm dugong and turtles. Population growth strains water, rainforest, land and mangroves. Overharvesting sometimes causes family and tribal disputes.
facts.note: From a 2018 funder profile.

facts.label: Funding reported
facts.value: Keepers of the Earth Fund (2018 profile); GEF Small Grants Programme from 2020; a full UNDP grant in 2022.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Mentors other conservation groups in East Are'are.

visitor.note: No visitor information found. Ask the association before any visit.

contact.note: No public contact found in the sources read.

consent.note: Prepared from published sources only. The association has not reviewed this profile.

open_questions: Where exactly are the protected mangrove, reef and seagrass areas, and what may be shown publicly?
Are the 2016 rules written down, and have they changed?
How have dugong and turtle numbers changed since the rules began?
What is the current relationship with Mai-Maasina Green Belt and Kira?
Does the group want visitors, and on what terms?
A 2020 WorldFish factsheet lists 'Ahetaha (Manawai)', which suggests Ahetaha is at or near Manawai Harbour. Is AWCA in the same locality as the Mai-Maasina Green Belt conservation village?

sites.name: Mai-Maasina Green Belt conservation village

location.note: Manawai Harbour is named, but no sourced coordinates were found.

sites.summary_en: A locally run conservation initiative in East Are'are with a conservation village at Manawai Harbour. A 2022 article reports UNDP-GEF funding for a training centre, toilets and hand-wash facilities, site mapping, a coastal no-take zone and a footpath.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Not stated.

facts.label: Legal status
facts.value: Not stated.

facts.label: Identity
facts.value: Described as representing the people of Are'are and run by local individuals, not an overseas organisation.

facts.label: Funded works reported
facts.value: Training centre, two ablution blocks and a hand-wash bay; site landscaping and GIS mapping; a 100-metre coastal no-go, no-take zone; a footpath and footbridge to the conservation village.
facts.note: The article does not make clear which works belong to Mai-Maasina Green Belt and which to its partner AWCA.

facts.label: Funding reported
facts.value: UNDP and the GEF Small Grants Programme.

facts.label: Partner
facts.value: Ahetaha Water Conservation Association.

visitor.note: A training centre and footpath were funded, which may suggest visitors or trainees. This is not confirmed. Ask first.

contact.note: A project officer is named in S05. Not republished here.

open_questions: What land and sea does the initiative look after, and who are the customary owners?
How does it relate to AWCA: separate groups, or one programme?
Who uses the training centre, and could it host student or visitor groups?
Where is the 100-metre no-take zone, and how is it enforced?
A 2020 WorldFish factsheet lists 'Ahetaha (Manawai)', which suggests Ahetaha is at or near Manawai Harbour. Is this conservation village in the same locality as AWCA?

sites.name: Roreaita Biodiversity Rainforest Conservation Association
sites.place_text: Central highlands, south-eastern corner of the Wairaha River Basin, 500-700 m above sea level

location.note: Described only by terrain and river basin. Highland forest locations may need generalising on request.

sites.summary_en: An association of four tribes protecting rainforest on tribal land in the highlands of East Are'are. It was registered in early 2018 and officially launched on 17 January 2023.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Not stated.

facts.label: Tribes and communities
facts.value: Ro-Rorowera, Re-Renamanu, Ai-Aimauma and Ta-Tawaenupu.

facts.label: Formed and launched
facts.value: Formed and registered in early 2018; official launch on 17 January 2023.

facts.label: Legal status
facts.value: Not stated. The article credits help with a 'protected area toolkit and application process' but does not say whether an application was made or approved.

facts.label: Support named
facts.value: A consultant with the Solomon Islands Rangers Association, plus mentoring from NGOs such as SICAN and provincial and national officers.

facts.label: Funding
facts.value: None named.

visitor.note: Remote highland tribal land. Treat as closed to visitors unless the four tribes invite you.

consent.note: Prepared from a single news article. The association has not reviewed this profile.

open_questions: How large is the forest, and what are its boundaries?
Did the association apply for protected-area status, and what happened?
Do the four tribes agree on how the area is described and mapped?
What species and habitats have been recorded?

sites.name: Puriasi Management Area
sites.place_text: Managed by the Mararo Community Based Organization

location.note: The area includes traditional taboo sites. Location is withheld on the public map until the custodians decide what to show.

sites.summary_en: A community-managed area of forested hillsides, mangrove shorelines and traditional taboo sites in East Are'are, run by the Mararo Community Based Organization. A 2020 article says it is becoming a breeding area for marine life and is threatened by nearby logging.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Size not stated.

facts.label: Habitats
facts.value: Thick forest on hillsides, mangrove shorelines, traditional taboo sites.

facts.label: Rules
facts.value: Certain catches and methods banned for three years, then a one-week opening for special occasions. Fines of up to SBD 500 for breaches.
facts.note: Reported in 2020. Rules may have changed.

facts.label: Reported outcomes
facts.value: The area is becoming a breeding area for marine life.
facts.note: Qualitative statement; no survey data in the source.

facts.label: Threats and pressures
facts.value: Nearby logging is described as a persistent threat.

facts.label: Support named
facts.value: WorldFish Solomon Islands did most of the site setup; Malaita Province fisheries division also named.
facts.note: The sentence names WorldFish for the Manaoba site; confirm it also applies to Puriasi.

facts.label: Second source
facts.value: A peer-reviewed study (catch recorded in 2017) describes a marine management area in the mangroves at Mararo, East Are'are, protecting invertebrates, and reports that logging began during sampling and threatens its marine habitats.
facts.note: Independent of S07. It names Mararo, not Puriasi; confirm that it describes the same area.

visitor.note: Includes taboo sites. Do not visit without explicit permission from the custodians.

contact.note: Contact via the Mararo Community Based Organization once they agree to be listed.

consent.note: Prepared from one 2020 article. Taboo-site information was deliberately not expanded.

open_questions: Are the 2020 rules still in force, and who enforces them?
What may be said publicly about the taboo sites, if anything?
Has the logging threat changed, and what is being done about it?
Does the organisation want the area on a public map at all?
Is the Mararo marine management area described in the 2022 study the same as Puriasi?

sites.name: Waisurione leatherback turtle nesting beach (Wai-Hau Conservation Foundation)
sites.place_text: Waisurione beach, spanning three tribal lands; Wai-Hau Conservation Foundation is based at Waisurione

location.note: Nesting beach. Locations of turtle nests invite egg poaching, so keep withheld on the public map unless the custodians decide otherwise.

sites.summary_en: A community-run leatherback turtle monitoring project on a nesting beach in West Are'are, led by the Wai-Hau Conservation Foundation. Local rangers patrol the beach, and a species management plan was being developed in 2018-19. A 2015 report called it one of the smaller rookeries in the Western Pacific.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: A 4.8 km beach.
facts.note: Beach length, not a protected-area size.

facts.label: Tribal lands
facts.value: Three tribal lands: Ausi (Wairaha), Au'vaura (Waisurione) and Po'otori (Hauhui).
facts.note: S19 names the second land 'Aena'ura'. Confirm spelling with the tribes.

facts.label: Management
facts.value: Wai-Hau Conservation Foundation Inc. runs the project, with community rangers.

facts.label: Rangers
facts.value: About 26 to 28 volunteer rangers elected by the community and local stakeholders in 2014-15.
facts.note: Numbers differ slightly across documents and are from 2014-15.

facts.label: Nesting
facts.value: Seven leatherback nests or emergences recorded in the 2015 season, May to July. The report called it one of the smaller rookeries in the Western Pacific.
facts.note: One season only. Current numbers unknown.

facts.label: Threats and pressures
facts.value: Storm erosion of the beach, risk of egg poaching, severe weather, and a territorial misunderstanding between tribal groups that limited monitoring on one side of the beach in 2015.

facts.label: Facilities
facts.value: A conservation centre was completed in 2015.

facts.label: Funding reported
facts.value: CEPF grants of about USD 15,400 (2016-17) and USD 18,000 (2018-19); Rufford Foundation and others earlier.

facts.label: Planning
facts.value: The 2018-19 grant aimed to produce a species management plan for Wai-Hau and southern Malaita. Whether it was finished is not stated.

facts.label: Legal status
facts.value: No protected-area registration found in the sources read.

visitor.note: Sources disagree: S19 says more than 15 tourists visited in 2015, while S21 mentions no ecotourism. Treat as closed to casual visits. Nesting beaches are fragile and poaching is a stated risk. Ask the Foundation.

consent.note: Prepared from published grant and project documents only.

open_questions: Is the project still active, and how many nests were recorded in recent seasons?
Was the species management plan finished, and is it public?
Which tribes and which beach sections are involved now, and how should each be named?
Does the Foundation want visitors, and under what rules?
How does the Foundation relate to Mai-Maasina Green Belt, whose anchor site is reported as Waihau?

sites.name: Apunepara Ha'amwaora Natural Resource Association (AHNRA)
sites.place_text: Maramasike Passage; training held at Waitomo village, Raroisu'u ward 21

location.note: Villages are named but not geolocated in the sources.

sites.summary_en: A tribal community association on the Maramasike Passage in Small Malaita working to protect forest and mangroves. In 2024 it trained about 30 rangers from five villages and began preparing a protected-area application. It also says it wants ecotourism and a carbon programme.

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Not stated.

facts.label: Participating villages
facts.value: Watoto, Sarawasi, Eliote, We'a and Malo'u.

facts.label: Focus
facts.value: Terrestrial forest and mangrove ecosystems, with mangrove species described as the flagship for conservation.

facts.label: Recent activity
facts.value: Protected-area management and ranger training on 20-23 May 2024, run by the Solomon Islands Rangers Association; about 30 rangers and representatives from five villages took part. A mangrove species survey was reported in 2024.

facts.label: Legal status
facts.value: Preparing a protected-area application. No registration reported.

facts.label: Threats and pressures
facts.value: Population growth and overharvesting, unsustainable logging, settlement expansion, betel nut plantations, slash-and-burn farming, sea level rise and saltwater intrusion.

facts.label: Stated aims
facts.value: Ecotourism, a carbon trade programme and sustainable livelihoods that maintain cultural practices.
facts.note: Aspirations, not operating activities.

facts.label: Support reported
facts.value: Solomon Islands Rangers Association; USAID's SCALE project (Winrock); a small grant.

visitor.note: The association says it wants ecotourism, but no visitor arrangements were found. Ask first.

contact.note: Founders are named in S22. Not republished here.

consent.note: Prepared from a single news article. Treat as a lead until custodians confirm.

open_questions: Which land and mangrove areas does AHNRA look after, and which tribe holds them?
Has the protected-area application been lodged, and what stage is it at?
Is there a map or boundary the association is ready to share?
What does the association want from tourism, and what would it refuse?

sites.name: Ohe'ohe Conservation Foundation
sites.place_text: East coast of southern Malaita, near Raeao

location.note: Point is the bay near Raeao, where custodian-supplied material places the Ohe'ohe Conservation Centre. Generalised to about 1 km; the exact location is held privately. It is NOT a boundary.

sites.summary_en: A community conservation foundation on the east coast of southern Malaita, near Raeao. Its sign asks people to protect mangroves, fauna and flora, and names Global GreenGrants Fund as its funder. Prepared from custodian-supplied material; little else is recorded yet.

facts.label: Sign
facts.value: "Conservation Matters: Protect our mangroves, fauna & flora"

facts.label: Sign: "Why it matters"
facts.value: mangroves protect our shores; fauna and flora sustain our eco-systems; biodiversity is our natural wealth

facts.label: Sign: your role
facts.value: "Your role: Preserve, Respect, Protect"

facts.label: Funding reported
facts.value: "Funded by: Global GreenGrants Fund"

facts.label: Area
facts.value: Not stated.

facts.label: Legal status
facts.value: Not stated.

facts.label: Management
facts.value: Not stated.

visitor.note: No visitor arrangements are recorded. Ask first.

consent.note: The material was supplied by a custodian for SouthSide. Consent for this profile is not yet recorded.

open_questions: What land, mangrove and sea area does the foundation look after, and who holds it?
When was the foundation formed, and is it registered?
What does the Global GreenGrants Fund support, and for how long?
What would the foundation want visitors and students to know, or not to do?
